items.body:
### App version
Installed Windows MSIX package: OpenAI.Codex 26.930.4958.0 (queried October 5, 2026). About-dialog version was not collected. Earlier log stack traces reference package 26.930.2377.0.

### Subscription
Not collected.

### Platform
Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0, x64. WSL Ubuntu-24.04 is used for local projects.

### Issue
The desktop app fails multiple times per day. The entire app screen displays “ChatGPT hit a snag...”; the window remains open. Completely quitting and reopening Codex does not restore usability. The user reports needing a full computer restart to recover, repeatedly interrupting work.

### Reproduction
1. Use Codex desktop normally on Windows with local/WSL projects. The exact triggering action is unknown.
2. The entire screen is replaced by the generic error.
3. Completely quit and reopen Codex: the error persists.
4. Restart the computer: the user reports this restores operation until another occurrence.

This is recurrent rather than a deterministic minimal reproduction. WSL shutdown was suggested but its effectiveness has not been verified.

### Expected behavior
The app remains usable. If the background engine fails, restarting the app should recover without requiring a full OS reboot, and the error should provide actionable diagnostic information.

### Diagnostic observations
Read-only inspection of local desktop logs established the following. These observations are not a confirmed root-cause diagnosis, and have not been precisely correlated to each visible error.

- On October 2, local stdio app-server connections repeatedly closed with code=4294967295, failureReason=unknown, signal=null. For example, at 18:54:04.678Z through 18:54:14.841Z, connection IDs advanced from 1594 to 1607 while replacement connections continued failing.
- On October 5 at 10:51:10.839Z, a local stdio connection closed with code=1073807364, failureReason=unknown, signal=null, connectionId=3778.
- October 5 logs show repeated ECONNRESET and ETIMEDOUT while watching/accessing project and worktree paths through \\wsl$\Ubuntu-24.04. Usernames and project paths are omitted here.
- On October 5 around 18:38–18:39Z, fatal_error_broadcasted entries include app-server exits with code=4294967295. The most recent backend warning included HTTP 409 Conflict from the remote-control websocket endpoint, with response detail “Remote app server already online”. Hostnames, installation/server/environment IDs and request IDs are omitted.
- At 2026-10-05T18:41:32.416Z, fatal_error_broadcasted recorded code=1, signal=null, initialized=false, transportKind=stdio. Subsequent entries at 18:41:33.473Z and 18:41:35.731Z recorded code=4294967295. Their most recent warning was “failed to load plugin: plugin is not installed”, plugin=code-review@openai-bundled. This warning may be incidental rather than causal.

The logs establish engine connection failures and unsuccessful recovery attempts. They do not establish whether WSL, remote-control registration conflicts, plugin loading, or another condition caused the original failures.

### Related reports
https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/41988 describes a surviving desktop window and app-server termination, but reports successful automatic recovery and a different exit code. This report adds persistent failure after a complete app quit/relaunch, repeated recovery failures, and newer package/log evidence.

### Privacy and provenance
Prepared with Codex at the user's explicit request using their reported symptoms and read-only local diagnostics. No full logs, conversation contents, credentials, usernames, project names, hostnames, or unique installation identifiers are attached.

items.body:
**Subject:** Codex on Windows: requested workspace-write became read-only — embedded exec policy resolution and child permission support

**Status:** Local request; not submitted.

**2026-10-05 diagnostic update:** Exact standalone 0.160.0 version/help and
fresh experimental schema export were inspected without RPC or a model turn.
The image matches the recorded SHA-256. The readiness response exposes only
ready/notConfigured/updateRequired; environment info exposes shell/default cwd;
environment status exposes connectivity; permission-profile listing exposes
IDs and whether selection is allowed (`permissionProfile/list`). These fields do not establish the exact
exec-selected executor, Windows sandbox level or policy restriction cause.
Current general subagent docs list sandbox_mode, while the pinned 0.160.0 V1
source projection omits it. Please resolve this release-specific difference.
The [local preflight report](docs/validation/exec-policy-provenance-preflight-0.160.0.md)
records scope and side effects. The five questions below remain open.

**Research refinement:** The local research in `responce.md` suggests a separate
app-server `thread/start` without `turn/start` as a possible partial runtime
snapshot. This is a proposal, not an executed diagnostic or an authoritative
support answer. No complete inspector was identified within the advertised CLI
and selected schemas inspected; this does not establish that no supported
inspector exists elsewhere. Please distinguish release-pinned support from
current documentation and confirm the procedure's limits for 0.160.0.

## Environment and observations

We are validating a custom-agent workflow on native Windows.

### Historical failing case

- Native CLI version: **0.159.3**.
- The exact backend serving that capture was **not identified**.
- Invocation used these options:

  ```text
  codex exec
    --ignore-user-config
    --strict-config
    --enable multi_agent
    --json
    --sandbox workspace-write
    -C <owned temporary fixture>
    <fixed task>
  ```

  This is a schematic invocation; the runner also supplied a fixture-specific trust override.

- The captured **parent policy was read-only before the child was spawned**.
- The child's role configuration requested `workspace-write`, but its captured policy was also `read-only`.
- Task evidence was present; the child's model and reasoning effort matched its configuration.
- This case remains a sandbox-policy validation failure.

### Current environment after upgrade

- Native standalone CLI is now **0.160.0**, independently verified.
- Verified standalone executable SHA-256:
  `fdda5fa3cf3fb3d000b876720742857676293e4315e4b045fae6f8bd7e866d1d`.
- The read-only `codex app-server daemon version` diagnostic reported:
  - `status: running`
  - `backend: pid`
  - `cliVersion: 0.160.0`
  - `managedCodexVersion: 0.160.0`
  - `appServerVersion: 0.160.0`
- This diagnostic describes the separate managed daemon. It does not bind ordinary embedded exec or explain its enforced policy.
- No fresh paid behavioral capture has been run after the upgrade.

### Checks already performed

Before the upgrade:

- `config/read` reported `sandbox_mode: workspace-write` from the user configuration layer.
- `configRequirements/read` returned `requirements: null`.
- That config read did **not** reproduce the historical invocation's CLI flags or session scope, so it does not explain the captured restriction.

The inspected 0.160.0 typed `thread/read` response did not expose a defined field for enforced-policy origin or serving-backend identity. We did not resume a thread or inspect private database files.

## Release-pinned source findings (0.160.0 only)

We inspected official release rust-v0.160.0 at commit
a956835d020762cb2b570053af06f643a11c0ecc. These are static source findings,
not a vendor answer or a measurement of the historical 0.159.3 run.

- Ordinary exec dispatch starts an embedded in-process app-server. Separate
  managed-daemon binding is not a prerequisite established by this source path.
- The legacy Windows path converts workspace-write to read-only when the
  effective Windows sandbox level is Disabled. This can occur with an explicit
  sandbox argument; we have not measured the relevant historical level.
- Requirements can constrain a configured profile; environment selection can
  supply the effective profile returned in the thread snapshot.
- The default sandbox-selection fallback and the core loader's separate
  requirements-constrained fallback are distinct paths. A default-only fallback
  must not be used to explain an explicit CLI sandbox request without tracing
  the actual resolution path.
- ThreadStartResponse includes snapshot sandbox and optional experimental
  activePermissionProfile. Exec's bootstrap conversion uses its local config
  permission profile, rather than response.sandbox, for that profile field.
- JSONL thread.started contains only thread_id. The non-JSON stderr sandbox
  summary also uses local config; it is not complete server-policy provenance.
- V1 child preparation reapplies the parent live permission snapshot after role
  setup. Its typed role override projection does not forward sandbox_mode or
  permission-profile fields. A role TOML declaration alone therefore does not
  establish role-specific enforcement in 0.160.0.

Pinned references:
[embedded route](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/a956835d020762cb2b570053af06f643a11c0ecc/codex-rs/exec/src/lib.rs#L986),
[Windows selection](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/a956835d020762cb2b570053af06f643a11c0ecc/codex-rs/config/src/config_toml.rs#L798),
[output conversion](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/a956835d020762cb2b570053af06f643a11c0ecc/codex-rs/exec/src/lib.rs#L1473),
[child preparation](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/a956835d020762cb2b570053af06f643a11c0ecc/codex-rs/core/src/agent/child_config.rs#L51),
[role projection](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/a956835d020762cb2b570053af06f643a11c0ecc/codex-rs/core/src/agent/role.rs#L36).

## Questions requiring an answer

### 1. How can we inspect embedded exec policy without a paid turn?

For native standalone 0.160.0, identify a supported command or API that shows
the policy resolved for the exact exec invocation, including:

- Whether the supplied CLI sandbox/ignore-user-config/strict-config options apply.
- The selected executor environment and effective Windows sandbox level/type.
- The requested policy, resolved configuration profile, and environment-effective
  thread/turn policy, with relevant writable roots and restriction source/precedence.
- How the evidence binds to the executable version and invocation/session.

Please provide method, parameters, response fields, schema and interpretation.
Can this be obtained before creating a thread or starting a model turn?
If it cannot, please state that limitation and the supported minimum procedure.

For the proposed separate app-server `thread/start` diagnostic, please provide:

- Exact launch arguments, `initialize` capability requirements, and request
  payloads supported by 0.160.0, including whether `ephemeral: true` is supported
  and what it guarantees.
- How to reproduce exec's resolved configuration, trust context, CLI overrides,
  permission-profile selection and executor environment. State any differences
  between the two launch paths rather than assuming equivalence.
- Which returned fields are observations of that newly created thread only,
  and whether any supported mechanism binds them to the exact embedded exec
  invocation being investigated.
- A list of unresolved fields after this procedure. A separate-thread snapshot
  alone cannot establish exact-exec provenance, Windows restriction cause or
  child-policy enforcement.

### 2. Is the Windows read-only transition intended?

Please confirm the supported behavior of explicit workspace-write when the
legacy Windows sandbox level is Disabled. How can we distinguish this platform
fallback from a managed requirement or an executor-environment restriction
without weakening policy or changing global configuration?

Please identify the observations needed to distinguish the Windows Disabled
fallback, default sandbox selection, the core loader's requirements-constrained
fallback, and an environment-selected profile. Explain which supported field
reveals the selected branch and restriction precedence, or state that this
information is unavailable.

We have not established that this condition caused the historical 0.159.3
failure. Please identify version-specific guidance for that historical analysis
separately; do not assume a mixed-version managed-daemon pairing served it.

### 3. Which policy output is supported as evidence?

ThreadStartResponse has snapshot policy fields, but ordinary exec JSONL does
not emit them in thread.started, and its bootstrap/human summary uses the local
configuration profile. Which supported surface exposes the actual responding
thread/turn policy and its source, including environment differences?

If suggesting config/read or thread/read, identify the exact fields and scope.
If suggesting logging, specify a stable allowlist and privacy-safe collection
procedure rather than a raw environment, configuration or transcript dump.
Proposed session.policy events are not assumed to exist.

For a `thread/start` snapshot, distinguish `sandbox`, `cwd`,
`runtimeWorkspaceRoots`, and optional experimental `activePermissionProfile`
from configuration inputs and profile catalog entries. An active profile's
`id`/`extends` does not by itself establish restriction origin or precedence;
`permissionProfile/list` describes available profiles and selection eligibility,
not the enforced policy of an existing exec thread.

Provide a field-by-field allowlist for any proposed `config/read`,
`configRequirements/read`, profile-list or thread response capture. Include only
necessary policy fields and sanitized identifiers/paths; do not request whole
configuration or requirements objects by default.

### 4. Are custom-agent sandbox restrictions supported in 0.160.0?

Please confirm whether sandbox_mode or permission-profile settings in a custom
agent TOML are supported runtime controls for V1 spawning. The inspected role
projection does not forward them, and parent runtime permissions are reapplied.

In particular, what supported mechanism makes a read-only child remain
read-only under a workspace-write parent? How can we prove requested and
effective child policy, parent lineage and restriction source without relying
only on role-file content? Please identify limitations or a version-specific
alternative; we need guidance before running role-specific behavioral gates.

Please name the exact supported method or event that exposes the child's
effective policy and parent linkage. If none is available in this release,
separate that observability limitation from whether a child restriction is
supported, and describe any required enforcement test and its side effects.

### 5. What are the diagnostic side effects?

Identify whether the proposed procedure creates/persists a thread, resumes
finished state, starts a model turn, writes metadata or requires a lifecycle
change. We need zero-model-turn, bounded read-only checks first. Preserve enforced
restrictions and existing configuration. Zero model turns must not be described
as a guarantee of no writes, network activity or other side effects.

For each step, explicitly identify:

- Model/provider requests, possible billing, and whether omitting `turn/start`
  prevents all model requests in the proposed procedure.
- Thread/session creation, rollout/database/metadata writes, logs and caches,
  including what ephemeral mode does and does not prevent.
- Execution-environment connection or startup, remote activity, MCP startup,
  hooks and authentication interactions. `environment/info` connects to an
  environment; do not classify it as a passive status-only read.
- Required permissions, initialization failures, shutdown/unsubscribe behavior,
  and any necessary cleanup, without resuming existing threads or altering
  global configuration or enforced restrictions.

Separate truly passive checks from no-model-turn thread creation and later
behavioral probes. Please supply a reviewable procedure before execution; this
request does not authorize the proposed thread creation or lifecycle changes.

## Requested outcome and acceptance

A supported evidence procedure must establish the ordinary embedded launch
route and selected executor, requested/resolved/environment-effective parent
policy and cause, and supported child-policy semantics. Matching daemon version
strings do not close these gaps. State any unavailable field or unavoidable
side effect explicitly.

Collect only sanitized allowlisted evidence tied to the relevant version and
invocation/session. Any later write-denial probe needs an owned disposable
target outside every effective writable root, including temporary directories.

Until accepted independent validation/review closes the preflight, it remains
BLOCKED. Historical L8 remains FAIL with seven cases NOT RUN; release NOT READY,

items.title: Daemon bootstrap reports success while its updater exits with SUN_LEN under a deep CODEX_HOME (Linux)

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
## Behaviour

On Linux with codex-cli 0.160.0, `app-server daemon bootstrap` successfully starts the managed app-server and records a daemon-updater PID, but the updater immediately exits when its Unix socket path exceeds the platform address limit. Its stderr contains `Error: path must be shorter than SUN_LEN`, and `daemon-updater.sock` never appears. The serving daemon survives, so an immediate PID-file check can incorrectly suggest that auto-update is working.

Observed in a private HOME under a pytest directory on 2026-10-03. No production daemon was stopped or restarted. The fixture's updater socket was longer than Linux's 108-byte Unix-address field. A short private HOME under disk TMPDIR produces a 99-byte updater address and is the proposed fixture workaround.

## Source

The updater binds its manual-update listener directly to `manual_update_socket_path()` in [update_loop.rs:118–128](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.160.0/codex-rs/app-server-daemon/src/update_loop.rs#L118).

That path is the updater PID-file path with a `.sock` extension, with no short-address mapping, in [lib.rs:993–995](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.160.0/codex-rs/app-server-daemon/src/lib.rs#L993).

The existing [deep control-socket path report](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/27765) describes daemon-client control addresses in 0.137/0.139 on macOS. This reproduction concerns the updater's separate socket in 0.160.0 on Linux; the app-server control socket itself works through its existing long-path fallback.

## Reproduction

1. Create a private HOME on disk with a long absolute path. Set `CODEX_HOME` to its `.codex` directory. Choose the length so `$CODEX_HOME/app-server-daemon/daemon-updater.sock` exceeds 108 bytes.
2. Copy the installed 0.160.0 app-server release into that private home's `packages/app-server-daemon/releases/0.160.0-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`, create `current` pointing at that release, and write that release name without a newline to `auto-update-version`. Never share writable package files or lifecycle state with the real HOME.
3. In the private `app-server-daemon/settings.json`, enable automatic updates and set shutdown grace to zero. Use a private config and no credentials.
4. Run the private binary with HOME, CODEX_HOME and TMPDIR explicitly set to private paths:

   ```sh
   "$private_codex" app-server daemon bootstrap
   ```

5. After bootstrap succeeds, read `app-server-daemon/daemon-updater.pid`, inspect that process, the updater socket, and `daemon-updater.stderr.log`.

Observed: the updater exits, the socket is absent, and stderr reports SUN_LEN; the daemon accepts a turn. Shortening only the private HOME makes the updater address fit. Stop only the private daemon and updater when finished.

## Expected

The updater should use a private short-address mapping for long paths, consistently with app-server control sockets. Bootstrap should not report a working updater merely because its PID record was published before startup failed. A regression should verify the updater stays alive and serves its socket after bootstrap with a long CODEX_HOME.

Environment: codex-cli 0.160.0 (npm, linux-x64 musl), Ubuntu, managed app-server daemon.

items.title: app-server rejects every turn with "invalid cwd" once the daemon's own working directory is deleted, even when the request cwd is absolute

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
## What happens

The shared app-server daemon starts with the working directory of the first `codex` invocation that spawns it. If that directory is later deleted (a removed git worktree, for example), every new `turn/start` on that daemon fails:

```
turn/start failed: invalid cwd: No such file or directory (os error 2) (code -32600)
```

This happens even though the turn's own `cwd` is an absolute path to a directory that exists. Every TUI attached to the daemon is affected until the daemon restarts. `codex resume <thread> --no-daemon` works around it for one session.

## Why

`resolve_request_cwd` (codex-rs/app-server/src/request_processors.rs:629, rust-v0.160.0) resolves the request cwd with `AbsolutePathBuf::relative_to_current_dir`:

```rust
fn resolve_request_cwd(cwd: Option<PathBuf>) -> Result<Option<AbsolutePathBuf>, JSONRPCErrorError> {
    cwd.map(|cwd| {
        AbsolutePathBuf::relative_to_current_dir(path_utils::normalize_for_native_workdir(cwd))
            .map_err(|err| invalid_request(format!("invalid cwd: {err}")))
    })
    .transpose()
}
```

`relative_to_current_dir` (codex-rs/utils/absolute-path/src/lib.rs:87) calls `std::env::current_dir()?` unconditionally, before it looks at whether `path` is already absolute:

```rust
pub fn relative_to_current_dir<P: AsRef<Path>>(path: P) -> std::io::Result<Self> {
    Ok(Self::resolve_path_against_base(
        path,
        std::env::current_dir()?,
    ))
}
```

On Linux, `getcwd` fails with ENOENT when the process's cwd has been unlinked. So an absolute request path is rejected because of the daemon's own cwd, which the path does not depend on. The same call is used for `turn/start` (turn_processor.rs:621, :928) and thread resume (thread_processor.rs:3877).

## Reproduce

1. With no daemon running (`codex app-server daemon stop`), run `mkdir /tmp/x && cd /tmp/x && codex`. This starts the daemon with cwd `/tmp/x`. Exit the TUI.
2. `rm -rf /tmp/x`
3. `cd ~/some/repo && codex`, then send any prompt. The turn fails with `invalid cwd`.

## Expected

An absolute request cwd resolves without consulting the process cwd. Only a relative request cwd needs `current_dir()`, and its error could say that the daemon's working directory no longer exists.

Possible fix: in `relative_to_current_dir`, return `from_absolute_path(path)` when `path.is_absolute()`, and call `current_dir()` only for relative input.

## Related

The managed daemon and its updater both inherit the spawning terminal's cwd (`codex app-server daemon start`, and `Daemon::stop` leaves `daemon-updater.pid` running). So after `stop` + `start`, the next update recreates the daemon in the deleted directory again; only `daemon bootstrap` replaces both processes. Starting the managed daemon from a stable directory (for example `$CODEX_HOME`) regardless of the caller's cwd would remove the whole class.

Environment: codex-cli 0.160.0 (npm, linux-x64 musl), Ubuntu, managed app-server daemon (`codex app-server --listen unix:// --managed-daemon`).

Related report: #41559 (a session whose own cwd was removed). This issue is a different trigger: the request cwd exists and is absolute, and only the daemon process's cwd is gone.

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Codex Desktop for Windows: `26.930.3930.0`

Bundled WSL runtime:

```text
codex-cli 0.160.0
```

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Plus

### What platform is your computer?

```text
Windows: 10.0.26200.9457 x64
WSL: 2.7.10.0
WSL distro: Ubuntu
WSL kernel: 6.18.33.2-2
```

Codex Desktop is configured to run the agent in WSL:

```toml
[desktop]
runCodexInWindowsSubsystemForLinux = true
integratedTerminalShell = "wsl"
```

### What issue are you seeing?

Codex works normally when the Desktop agent runtime is Windows-native, but in WSL mode model requests repeatedly fail with `error sending request` / `Reconnecting...`.

I was able to narrow this down to a very specific difference between the two IPv4 A records currently returned for `chatgpt.com`.

On this machine:

```text
chatgpt.com -> 104.18.32.47
chatgpt.com -> 172.64.155.209
```

A plain HTTPS client can reach **both** addresses successfully from both WSL and Windows. However, Codex 0.160.0 in WSL succeeds when `chatgpt.com` is pinned to `104.18.32.47`, and hangs when it is pinned to `172.64.155.209`.

This does not appear to be a general DNS, TCP, TLS, MTU, authentication, or Cloudflare reachability failure.

#### Baseline checks

DNS and HTTPS from WSL work:

```text
getent ahostsv4 chatgpt.com

104.18.32.47    STREAM chatgpt.com
172.64.155.209  STREAM
```

`auth.openai.com/oauth/token` is reachable from WSL and returns an expected HTTP response when queried with the wrong method.

Authentication is readable by Codex:

```text
$ codex login status
Logged in using ChatGPT
```

No proxy or custom CA environment variables are set.

#### Failure from Codex

With the WSL Codex binary:

```bash
CODEX_HOME=/mnt/c/Users/<user>/.codex \
CODEX_SQLITE_HOME=/home/<user>/.codex/sqlite \
codex exec --skip-git-repo-check "Reply with exactly: OK"
```

I get errors such as:

```text
ERROR codex_models_manager::manager: failed to refresh available models:
Connection failed: error sending request

ERROR rmcp::transport::worker:
http/request failed: error sending request for url
(https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/ps/mcp)

ERROR: Reconnecting... 2/5
ERROR: Reconnecting... 3/5
ERROR: Reconnecting... 4/5
ERROR: Reconnecting... 5/5

warning: Falling back from WebSockets to HTTPS transport.
workspace routing discovery failed
```

The failure continues after the WebSocket -> HTTPS fallback, so this is not limited to WebSocket upgrade handling.

With `RUST_LOG=trace`, the relevant sequence is repeatedly:

```text
reqwest::connect: starting new connection: https://chatgpt.com/
hyper_util::client::legacy::connect::http:
Http::connect; scheme=Some("https"), host=Some("chatgpt.com"), port=None

hyper_util::client::legacy::pool:
checkout dropped for ("https", chatgpt.com)
```

The client reports use of system root certificates; there is no custom CA override.

#### A/B test: curl reaches both addresses

From WSL:

```bash
curl -4 --resolve "chatgpt.com:443:104.18.32.47" \
  --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 10 \
  -sS -o /dev/null \
  -w 'http=%{http_code} remote=%{remote_ip} connect=%{time_connect}s tls=%{time_appconnect}s total=%{time_total}s\n' \
  https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/
```

Result:

```text
http=403 remote=104.18.32.47 connect=0.025356s tls=0.059468s total=0.090174s
```

For the other address:

```text
http=403 remote=172.64.155.209 connect=0.028862s tls=0.070166s total=0.104953s
```

The same `curl --resolve` test also succeeds from Windows against both addresses:

```text
104.18.32.47:
http=403 connect=0.037784s tls=0.107448s total=0.160706s

172.64.155.209:
http=403 connect=0.036878s tls=0.096077s total=0.138953s
```

So both endpoints are reachable and complete TLS normally.

#### A/B test: Codex behaves differently per A record

Pinning `chatgpt.com` to the first address:

```text
104.18.32.47 chatgpt.com
```

then running the same `codex exec` command succeeds immediately:

```text
OpenAI Codex v0.160.0
...
user
Reply with exactly: OK
codex
OK
```

Pinning it instead to:

```text
172.64.155.209 chatgpt.com
```

causes the same `codex exec` invocation to hang until an external 30-second timeout terminates it.

Switching back to:

```text
104.18.32.47 chatgpt.com
```

restores working Codex requests.

This is currently the reliable workaround.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

On a Windows + WSL2 machine using ChatGPT authentication and Codex CLI 0.160.0:

1. Confirm `chatgpt.com` resolves to both `104.18.32.47` and `172.64.155.209`.
2. Confirm both addresses are individually reachable with `curl --resolve`.
3. Pin `chatgpt.com` to `104.18.32.47` in WSL `/etc/hosts`.
4. Run:
   ```bash
   codex exec --skip-git-repo-check "Reply with exactly: OK"
   ```
5. Observe that Codex succeeds.
6. Replace the hosts entry with:
   ```text
   172.64.155.209 chatgpt.com
   ```
7. Run the exact same command.
8. Observe that Codex hangs/retries and does not complete before an external timeout.

Without an `/etc/hosts` override, normal DNS returns both A records and the WSL Codex runtime can repeatedly enter the failing reconnect state.

### What is the expected behavior?

Codex should be able to use either reachable A record, or retry/fallback to another resolved address when a connection attempt is not making progress.

In particular, when `curl` from the same WSL environment can establish TCP/TLS and receive an HTTP response from both addresses in ~100 ms, Codex should not hang indefinitely on one of them.

The address-selection / connection-pool path should fail over rather than repeatedly reconnecting to an unusable candidate.

### Additional information

- No `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, `ALL_PROXY`, custom CA, or Git proxy is configured.
- Changing WSL MTU from 1500 to 1488 did not change the Codex failure.
- `curl` reaches both A records from WSL and from Windows, so this does not look like a simple ISP route failure.
- The WSL resolver in this reproduction returns IPv4 A records; the observed behavior here is **not** the IPv6-first case described in #13406.
- This looks related to the broader class of `curl`-works / Codex-HTTP-client-stalls reports such as #34397, but this reproduction adds a deterministic A/B boundary between two IPv4 A records.

During diagnosis I also encountered the separate WSL state-location issue tracked in #31426: placing SQLite state under `/mnt/c/.../.codex` can prevent the app-server from initializing. I worked around that independently using a WSL-native `CODEX_SQLITE_HOME`, after which the network failure above remained reproducible. I am reporting the network/address-selection behavior separately so the two problems are not conflated.

I can provide a sanitized full `RUST_LOG=trace` capture if useful.

labels.name: bug

labels.name: mcp

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using?

Before recovery: ChatGPT desktop hosting Codex, version **26.928.21956**, build **12404**.
After recovery: version **26.928.31416**, build **12553**.

Versions were read from app bundle metadata. Restart also changed the installed app version; this is not a controlled same-version restart experiment.

### What subscription do you have?

Not disclosed for privacy; no account or billing data is included.

### What platform is your computer?

macOS **26.5.1 (25F80)**, Apple Silicon / arm64.
Xcode **26.6 (17F113)**; Apple clang **21.0.0 (clang-2100.1.1.101)**; macOS SDK **26.5**.

### What issue are you seeing?

After approximately five days of desktop uptime, Xcode builds stalled at **Planning / Discovering version info for clang**, before compiling any application source. Terminal xcodebuild also stalled at compiler discovery with signing disabled. Restarting only the build service did not resolve the problem.

Fresh nonblocking pipes could accept only **512 bytes** and would not expand. Most observed PIPE file descriptors belonged to the desktop app's descendant process tree. After restarting/updating the desktop app, pipe capacity and compiler controls recovered; the application build also succeeded according to the user.

| Measurement | Before restart/update | After restart/update |
|---|---:|---:|
| System-visible PIPE file descriptors | 4,351 | 871 |
| Processes in desktop app tree, including root | 546 | 26 |
| PIPE descriptors in desktop app tree | 3,622 | 119 |
| PIPE descriptors outside that tree | 729 | 752 |
| Fresh pipe usable capacity | 512 bytes | 65,536 bytes |
| clang with concurrent stdout/stderr collection | Exit 0, 0.0148 s | Exit 0, 0.0108 s |
| clang with sequential stdout/stderr collection | Timeout after 5 s | Exit 0, 0.0321 s |

Before recovery, the app tree contained 169 bundled CUA node processes, 102 node_repl processes, and 51 launcher/server pairs for chrome-devtools-mcp. One bundled Codex server held 923 PIPE descriptors. Expected process counts for persistent chats were not established.

These are descriptor endpoints, not unique pipes or allocated pipe-buffer bytes. Process-tree attribution includes tools/plugins and transient diagnostics. Snapshot counts alone do not prove a leak.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

The exact trigger for accumulating the desktop resources has not been isolated. The following diagnostic reproduces the downstream compiler deadlock while the affected pipe-pressure state is present, without accessing an application project, private source or account data.

1. In a long-running desktop session with many tool runtimes, measure process/PIPE counts using `ps` and `lsof` locally. Do not publish raw output.
2. Run this diagnostic. Before recovery it reports 512-byte pipe capacity, successful concurrent collection, and a sequential-collection timeout. After recovery it reports 65,536-byte capacity and successful collection in both modes.
3. Restart the desktop app and repeat. Record app versions before/after to distinguish restart from update. Keep Xcode, source and caches unchanged where possible.

```python
import json
import os
import signal
import subprocess
import sys
import time

for block in (512, 1024, 4096, 16384, 32768, 65536):
    r, w = os.pipe()
    os.set_blocking(w, False)
    total = 0
    try:
        while True:
            total += os.write(w, b'x' * block)
    except BlockingIOError:
        print('write block:', block, 'accepted bytes:', total)
    finally:
        os.close(r)
        os.close(w)

clang = subprocess.check_output(['xcrun', '--find', 'clang'], text=True).strip()
sdk = subprocess.check_output(
    ['xcrun', '--sdk', 'macosx', '--show-sdk-path'], text=True).strip()
argv = [clang, '-v', '-E', '-dM', '-arch', 'arm64',
        '-isysroot', sdk, '-x', 'c', '-c', '/dev/null']
t = time.monotonic()
result = subprocess.run(argv, capture_output=True, timeout=10)
print('concurrent:', result.returncode, round(time.monotonic() - t, 4),
      'stdout bytes:', len(result.stdout), 'stderr bytes:', len(result.stderr))

worker = (
    'import subprocess,json,sys; '
    'p=subprocess.Popen(json.loads(sys.argv[1]),'
    'stdout=subprocess.PIPE,stderr=subprocess.PIPE); '
    'out=p.stdout.read();err=p.stderr.read();p.wait();'
    'print(p.returncode,len(out),len(err))'
)
p = subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, '-c', worker, json.dumps(argv)],
                     stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE,
                     start_new_session=True)
t = time.monotonic()
try:
    out, err = p.communicate(timeout=5)
    print('sequential:', p.returncode, round(time.monotonic() - t, 4),
          out.decode().strip())
except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
    os.killpg(p.pid, signal.SIGTERM)  # Only this disposable diagnostic group.
    p.communicate(timeout=5)
    print('sequential: timeout after 5 seconds')
```

The compiler command operates on `/dev/null`. Successful controls produced 15,789 stdout bytes and 4,829 stderr bytes. Independent C/Objective-C/C++ concurrent controls and a Swift DispatchIO control also succeeded.

### What is the expected behavior?

Desktop tool runtimes and stdio connections should have bounded lifecycles/resource use. Prolonged desktop use should not exhaust a global pipe-buffer resource and stall unrelated developer tools. The app should release unused runtimes/descriptors or reuse them as appropriate.

### Additional information

During the failure, sampled clang stacks ended in:

```text
clang::driver::Command::Print
llvm::raw_ostream::write
llvm::raw_fd_ostream::write_impl
write
```

SWBBuildService's sampled main thread was idle in its run loop. Clang completed promptly when both streams were drained concurrently.

The leading explanation is global pipe-buffer pressure exposing a sequential-output-collection deadlock in the build tool:

- Apple's [XNU pipe implementation](https://github.com/apple-oss-distributions/xnu/blob/main/bsd/kern/sys_pipe.c) gates pipe-buffer growth on `amountpipekva < maxpipekva`. Relevant memory-limit sysctls were unavailable on this production kernel, so buffer-budget exhaustion is inferred from capacity probes and recovery, not directly measured.
- Public SwiftBuild [release/6.3 Process.swift](https://github.com/swiftlang/swift-build/blob/release/6.3/Sources/SWBUtil/Process.swift) collects stdout then stderr sequentially; [main](https://github.com/swiftlang/swift-build/blob/main/Sources/SWBUtil/Process.swift) collects them concurrently. This explains a matching mechanism; the installed Xcode binary was not proven to correspond exactly to that release branch.

Related: #35582 already discusses retained CUA/MCP workers and global pipe-pool pressure. This report adds a specific Xcode compiler-discovery failure, measured pipe capacity, a project-independent compiler reproduction, and quantified before/after recovery. It should not be assumed to establish the same automation-specific retention path.

Important limitations:

- Restart coincided with app bundle build 12404 changing to 12553. Restart-only and update effects cannot be separated; this does not prove the newer build fixes a particular leak.
- The after-restart resource counts and compiler controls were independently measured. Successful full application build is user-reported; no successful build log was collected.
- No growth series or controlled count of expected persistent chats was collected. The exact retention/cleanup owner remains unknown.
- Other intervening user actions were not independently monitored.

Please investigate lifecycle/pooling of per-chat CUA/REPL and stdio MCP runtimes and the global pipe-resource impact during extended desktop use.

Privacy: this report contains only product versions, aggregate measurements, symbolic stack frames and a generic reproduction. It includes no names, usernames, email addresses, user paths, project identity/source, machine identifiers, process/chat/session IDs, location, screenshots, raw logs, credentials or billing details. ```

### What issue are you seeing?

Two separate $200/month Pro accounts showed substantially different weekly quota depletion during October 3–4, 2026. I am reporting an unexplained usage-accounting discrepancy, not a confirmed billing bug.

Both workloads predominantly used GPT-6.1-Sol with High reasoning. The second account was busier, but its quota depleted disproportionately faster. Fast mode and Astra were used only sparingly according to my usage.

All times below are Europe/Prague (UTC+02:00). Account identifiers are omitted from this public draft; the uploaded investigation thread contains the context.

Endpoint-aligned comparison from local session logs and account-specific hourly reports:

| Metric | Account A | Account B |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Complete hourly buckets | Oct 3 06:00 through Oct 4 08:00 inclusive (27 hours) | Oct 4 12:00 through 19:00 inclusive (8 hours) |
| Weekly quota remaining | 96% → 6% | 83% → 1% |
| Quota consumed | 90 percentage points | 82 percentage points |
| Average quota consumed/hour | 3.33 percentage points | 10.25 percentage points |
| Requests/hour | 687 | 1,238 |
| Total tokens/hour (input + output; cached input included in input) | 97.02 million | 181.37 million |
| Uncached input tokens/hour | 2.90 million | 4.30 million |
| Output tokens/hour (reasoning included) | 379,029 | 684,426 |
| Cached share of input | 97.00% | 97.62% |

Quota endpoints are the last observations in the immediately preceding hour and the final included hour, rather than measurements exactly on the hour boundaries.

Account B's quota depletion/hour was approximately 3.08× Account A's. Its request rate was approximately 1.80×, uncached input/hour 1.48×, and output/hour 1.81×.

A model-aware workload estimate using published Standard Codex credit rates gives about 1.64× more weighted activity/hour on Account B, implying approximately 1.88× more quota per estimated weighted unit. This is only a diagnostic proxy: published purchased-credit rates do not define the included subscription quota formula, and these figures are not actual credits spent or invoice charges.

Please investigate whether this difference is expected or reflects an account entitlement, speed multiplier, metering, or quota-accounting problem.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Uploaded thread: 01a10631-3366-7592-88b2-8d180a3d7f8f

### What is the expected behavior?

Accounts with the same $200 Pro entitlement should receive consistent quota accounting for comparable activity under the same model and speed settings.

I understand that different workloads can consume quota differently and that raw token counts alone do not determine included quota consumption. Please explain the observed difference using the actual server-side accounting rules, or correct an entitlement/metering problem if one is found.

In particular, please verify both accounts' effective weekly entitlements, speed tiers/multipliers actually applied to requests, any other usage sharing the quota, and the usage ledger for October 3–4, 2026.

### Additional information

Checks completed during the local investigation:

- The user confirms both subscriptions are $200 Pro; local request records report plan_type=pro.
- Most requests used GPT-6.1-Sol High. The second account had a smaller Astra request share in the wider displayed windows (about 5.6% vs 7.3%).

- No weekly reset occurred inside the compared periods. Both reported reset times were approximately October 9, 2026, 23:13 Europe/Prague.
- No request in the selected windows had input above 272,000 tokens.

items.title: [macOS app] Readable local chat rejects submissions with thread_not_found; archive/unarchive restores loaded state

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Desktop release `26.930.31730` (build `12947`), verified from the installed application metadata and corroborated by the desktop session log. The About dialog was not inspected. The affected thread's stored runtime version is `0.159.0-alpha.12.1`; this is session metadata, not a fresh executable-version check.

### What subscription do you have?

Not collected for this report.

### What platform is your computer?

macOS `27.0.1`, Apple Silicon. Requested `uname -mprs` output: `Darwin 27.0.0 arm64 arm`. Affected chat host: `local`; stored history mode: `paginated`.

### What issue are you seeing?

An existing local chat remained listed in the sidebar and its recent history was readable, but submitting a new message repeatedly failed:

```text
thread not found: <affected-thread>
```

Desktop logs show JSON-RPC `-32600` with `failureReason=thread_not_found` on `turn/start` and `mcpServerStatus/list`, while `thread/read` and history pagination calls for the same thread succeeded.

The saved thread was not archived. Its rollout file existed and was readable (approximately 22 MB), and the thread API reported `notLoaded`. Simply navigating to the chat again did not change the reported `notLoaded` state. Archive → unarchive → reopen subsequently triggered a successful `thread/resume`, and independent status checks reported `idle`.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

**Reproduction status:** the submission failure repeated in one affected existing chat. A reliable way to put a fresh chat into the same broken state has not been established. The steps below reproduce the failure only when that state is already present.

**Preconditions:** a persistent local chat with completed turns, readable history, `archived=false`, and runtime status `notLoaded`, while the desktop still allows submission. No original prompt or private transcript is required to describe the failure.

1. Select an existing local chat that has completed previous turns.
2. Attempt to submit a new message. For a maintainer retest, use a neutral diagnostic input such as `Reply with OK.`; that prompt was not used in this incident, and prompt independence has not been experimentally verified.
3. Observe `thread not found: <affected-thread>`.
4. Retry submission: the same error recurs.
5. Read the chat through the thread-reading interface: recent completed turns are still accessible.
6. Reopen the chat through navigation: it remains `notLoaded`.
7. Archive the affected unloaded chat, unarchive it, and reopen it.
8. Observe a successful `thread/resume` and status `idle`.

**Observed lifecycle clue:** the same chat had a successful `thread/resume` earlier, followed by a successful `thread/unsubscribe` approximately seven minutes before the failed submissions. No intervening `thread/resume` response for this chat was recorded. Two `No promise for request ID` errors appeared immediately after the unsubscribe responses; their request IDs were not correlated, so they are a clue rather than an established cause. The action that initiated unsubscribe and whether it caused the loss of runtime state remain unknown.

**Maintainer regression-test proposal (not executed):** use a synthetic saved chat in an isolated fixture; remove its loaded runtime session through a test hook while keeping its history and the desktop's displayed chat/composer state. Attempt submission through the desktop. Assert that the client resumes the chat and waits for success before `turn/start`, rather than surfacing `thread_not_found`. This isolates the suspected stale-state boundary; merely calling `turn/start` against an unloaded fixture is not by itself proof of a desktop bug.

For an already initialized app-server test connection, the relevant request shapes are:

```jsonl
{"id":1,"method":"thread/read","params":{"threadId":"<synthetic-saved-thread-id>","includeTurns":false}}
{"id":2,"method":"turn/start","params":{"threadId":"<synthetic-saved-thread-id>","input":[{"type":"text","text":"Reply with OK.","text_elements":[]}]}}
```

Send these sequentially and await each response. The placeholder must refer to a real synthetic fixture, not a randomly invented ID. These shapes were checked against the public protocol schema; this is a diagnostic sketch, not a tested end-to-end reproducer. Use a stubbed model in the fixture so a successful submission does not start real model work.

### What is the expected behavior?

A saved, readable, unarchived chat should be resumed before the client sends operations that require a loaded session. If the runtime session has disappeared, the client should reconcile its cached state and offer recovery or resume the existing chat safely. Users should not need an archive/unarchive cycle to restore an existing conversation.

### Additional information

Sanitized diagnostic timeline from the same desktop session. Absolute timestamps are omitted; elapsed times are rounded relative to the affected chat's successful unsubscribe. Every row refers to the same chat, aliased `<affected-thread>`.

| Approximate elapsed time | Operation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | `thread/unsubscribe` | Success |
| +6m 35s | `turn/start` | `-32600`, `thread_not_found` |
| +6m 42s | `mcpServerStatus/list` | `-32600`, `thread_not_found` |
| +6m 42s | `turn/start` | `-32600`, `thread_not_found` |
| +7m 08s | `thread/read` | Success |
| +7m 08s | `thread/turns/list` | Success |
| +8m 22s | `thread/archive` | Success |
| +8m 23s | `thread/unarchive` | Success |
| +8m 24s | `thread/resume` | Success |

**Recovery verification:** archive/unarchive was performed through the desktop's supported thread-management tools. After reopening, both `wait_threads` and `list_threads` reported `idle`; the latest completed turn remained readable. No new prompt was sent merely to test recovery, so a subsequent successful `turn/start` was not independently verified. No databases or transcript contents were manually edited.

**Possible cause, unconfirmed:** disagreement between the client's cached chat state and the app-server's loaded-session state. The evidence establishes the read/start mismatch and successful reload, not the cause of the original unload.

**Related reports and duplicate search:** searched the issue tracker for `thread not found` together with `archive`, `unarchive`, and `unsubscribe`. #30710 describes a Windows stored-chat submission/resume race; #42604 describes macOS Goal/multi-agent history desynchronization; #45213 describes a Windows Goal chat with successful reads and failed start/interrupt; #39179 describes Windows archive/path-resolution failures. This incident adds a macOS case on the version above, with a successful unsubscribe before the failures and successful archive/unarchive/resume recovery. A common root cause is not established. If maintainers consider this the same defect, these findings can be added to the existing report instead of opening another issue.

**Privacy:** no names, email addresses, account IDs, full thread/session/request IDs, device names, IP addresses, private paths/URLs, project details, original prompts, conversation contents, screenshots, credentials, or raw logs are included. Absolute event timestamps and the exact transcript size are also omitted. The version/platform details, operation names, error codes, relative timing, and public issue references are retained for diagnosis. Session IDs and subscription/token/context-window usage were not included; no quota or context-window failure is asserted.

Prepared using the [Codex App issue template](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/1-codex-app.yml) and [OpenAI's contribution guidance](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/docs/contributing.md): environment, actual/expected behavior, reproduction limits, redacted diagnostics, and related reports are included.

### What version of the Codex App are you using

Desktop app bundle `com.openai.codex`, version 26.930.51102, build 13100. Installed bundle display name is ChatGPT; the task is running in Codex.

### What subscription do you have

### What platform is your computer

macOS 27.0.1, build 26A434.

### What issue are you seeing

The supported built-in Browser tool refuses a read-only accessibility read of the already-open `https://www.nytimes.com/` tab. The user provided a screenshot showing the exact origin `https://www.nytimes.com` with Browsing set to **Always allow** and reported that browser control was enabled. A direct retry through the same built-in browser after this permission change returned the same denial.

The error is returned by the Browser tool, not observed in the publisher page. No page content is returned, so these attempts do not establish an NYT HTTP rejection, CAPTCHA, authentication failure or publisher-side bot block.

Exact error:

```text
Browser Use rejected this action due to browser security policy. Reason: The site-safety policy blocks this action; no user permission prompt or Auto-review was attempted. Browser use is not permitted on https://www.nytimes.com. The agent must not attempt to achieve the same outcome via workaround, indirect execution, raw CDP or browser commands, alternate browser surfaces, or policy circumvention. Proceed only with a materially safer alternative that does not require this blocked browser action; if none exists, stop and request user input.
```

### What steps can reproduce the bug

1. In the desktop app's built-in browser, manually open `https://www.nytimes.com/` and sign in.
2. Enable browser control and set `https://www.nytimes.com` to Browsing **Always allow** in Settings > Browser.
3. Ask Codex to read the NYT page using the supported in-app Browser capability.
4. After selecting the existing tab, request its accessibility tree using the documented Browser runtime's `tab.ax.write()` operation.
5. Observe the site-safety denial before any page content, user permission prompt or Auto-review result is returned.

The failed retry was observed on October 6, 2026 in Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh. It occurred after the user reported changing permissions and supplied the screenshot. No additional repeated attempts or alternate retrieval methods were used after that retry.

Feedback session ID: `01a0a003-a20b-7f72-bfab-f5b4a7f6ca45`

Local application logs confirm a successful feedback upload for this session at `2026-10-05T17:26:55Z` (October 6, 00:26:55 Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh), with `attachments_failed=false`. A separate feedback-event ID was not exposed in the inspected logs.

### What is the expected behavior

If NYT read-only browser access is supported, honor the website permission or present the supported approval flow. If a stricter policy intentionally disallows access, explain which restriction controls the decision, why Always allow cannot resolve it, and how the user can request review or recover through a supported path.

Please investigate whether this is intentional site classification, an incorrect denial, or inconsistent permission/policy state. This report requests diagnosis and a supported resolution, not a policy bypass.

### Additional information

- Control tests: full article text was readable from FT and Washington Post through the same built-in Browser tool. Later temporary research-agent contexts also successfully read articles from those two publishers.
- A read-only inspection found no `browser_use` settings in the local user config. The checked user/system requirements files and project browser config were absent. This does not rule out app-level or managed policy.
- A targeted search for `repo:openai/codex nytimes browser` returned no existing issue at preparation time.
- Similar symptoms on other sites: https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/48382 and https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/48175 . These are related reports, not proof of the same root cause.
